question: How many phases does the PRD v2 append to simple-login.integration take, and how is the work split between them?

options.label: three: rig and service tests, Home, Rooms
options.consequence: simple-login.integration.3 builds the PostgreSQL rig, the booking-api@v1 replay and the API-level Success tests (~340 lines, 7 tasks); .4 adds the time helpers and the Home tests (AC-2.1, AC-2.5, US-6, ~250 lines); .5 the Rooms tests with London's clock-change days (US-4, US-5, AC-4.4, ~300 lines). Each fits one sitting; .4 and .5 differ in tier, so no merge candidate.

options.label: two: rig, then every browser test
options.consequence: The browser phase would be ~550 lines and 10 or more tasks, over one review sitting.

options.label: four: clock-change days on their own
options.consequence: Rooms (~200 lines) and clock-change days (~120 lines) would share tier and contracts with no third phase depending on one alone, and merged fit one sitting: a merge candidate pair under the sizing floor with no named reason to keep it split.

chosen: three: rig and service tests, Home, Rooms
why: Interfaces-first puts the shared rig first: the database of its own, the service started through its documented command, the API helpers, then the tests that use them. The browser work splits by screen because Home's tests make their bookings through booking-api@v1 and need no Rooms screen, while the Rooms tests need the time helpers .4 writes. Sizes are estimates from the shipped e2e files (414 lines today) and the strings the tests must compute.

question: Bookings now persist across runs of the suite (Q-073): how does a test run get a database, or slots, that no earlier run or developer has touched?

options.label: a database of its own per run
options.consequence: Playwright's global setup runs `npm --prefix backend run db:up`, then drops and re-creates `meeting_rooms_e2e` on the backend's Compose service through the `pg` package (a root devDependency) and starts the service with DATABASE_URL naming it. Every run starts empty and `meeting_rooms` keeps the developer's bookings. It assumes the service creates its tables in an empty database at start, which no contract states: a request entry asks.

options.label: the default database, free slots found through booking-api@v1
options.consequence: No new dependency and no assumption, but the tests write into the developer's `meeting_rooms`, a developer's booking can take a slot a test computed, and no test can assert '(no bookings)' or an exact Rooms day.

options.label: a database per test file
options.consequence: Stronger isolation, but the worker-scoped service would restart for every file, and the rig would manage several databases for no criterion that needs it.

chosen: a database of its own per run
why: The conventions' Local database section already gives the backend's tests databases of their own on that service and keeps them off `meeting_rooms`; the integration's tests do the same. Creating and dropping a database is a server operation that touches none of the backend's tables, so the schema stays the backend's (Q-073 rules out writing its tables). The `meeting_rooms` user can create databases (the backend's tests do; booking-store-postgres measured 36 ms a database). Inside a run, each test books on dates and rooms no other test uses. The gap is whether `npm --prefix backend start` creates its tables in an empty database: recorded as a request on booking-api@v1, with contingent phases none, because either answer keeps the phase set (a separate schema command would be run by the same global setup). A backend answer that the schema exists only through Compose's first-start scripts would have made the default database with free slots the better choice.

question: How does the browser suite's backend fixture start and restart the real service once it runs on PostgreSQL?

options.label: npm --prefix backend start, in its own process group
options.consequence: The rig depends only on the command the conventions document (needs the database up, reads DATABASE_URL, PORT pinned to 3000); a restart stops the whole group, as scripts/dev.mjs already does, and waits for port 3000 to close.

options.label: keep spawning backend/src/server.ts
options.consequence: One process to stop, as shipped, but the rig names a file inside backend/, which this node does not own and whose start-up may change with PostgreSQL.

chosen: npm --prefix backend start, in its own process group
why: simple-login.integration does not own any code under backend/ (node header), and the conventions' Local database section names `npm --prefix backend start` as the service's start command. scripts/dev.mjs shows the process-group stop works for npm-started children on this laptop. Evidence that the backend's start script adds work a test must not pay for on every restart would have kept the direct spawn.

question: Where do the root scripts start PostgreSQL for `npm run dev`, `npm test` and `npm run e2e`?

options.label: chained in package.json, and again in the e2e global setup
options.consequence: `dev` becomes `npm --prefix backend run db:up && node scripts/dev.mjs`; `test` runs `db:up` before the dev runner's test and the browser suite; the global setup runs it too, so `npm run e2e` works alone. scripts/dev.mjs and its tested process handling stay as shipped. No root db:down: the README names `npm --prefix backend run db:down`.

options.label: inside scripts/dev.mjs
options.consequence: One place for `dev`, but it changes the tested runner, its tests then need Docker for the failure case too, and `test` and `e2e` still need their own call.

chosen: chained in package.json, and again in the e2e global setup
why: Q-074 and the conventions say every node starts the database through `npm --prefix backend run db:up`, which picks `docker compose` or `docker-compose` and returns once healthy; on this laptop only docker-compose 5.6.1 exists, so no root script calls Docker itself. db:up is idempotent, so calling it twice in `npm test` costs a health check.

question: Which booking-api@v1 fixtures does the proxy replay extend to, against the real service on the real clock?

options.label: the 15 decided before any clock or stored-booking rule
options.consequence: Eight 400s, four 401s (my-bookings-expired-token through the shipped restart), cancel-unknown, cancel-malformed-id and book-too-long: 24 exact replays with the shipped nine. book-too-long holds because BOOKING_TOO_LONG is order 3 of POST, before the clock's orders 4 and 5.

options.label: the 14 Q-069 named
options.consequence: Leaves out book-too-long, a fixture the running service answers as written under every clock and state.

options.label: all 35 through a seeded database
options.consequence: Not possible: the service runs on the real clock and the fixtures fix theirs; seeding fixed ids would write the backend's tables.

chosen: the 15 decided before any clock or stored-booking rule
why: A reference model of the contract's check orders answered each fixture's request under 7 clocks from 2026-11-01 to 2028-11-01 and two stored states (none; 78,912 random-id bookings in every room): exactly 15 answer as written in every condition. Q-069's count of 14 missed book-too-long. The rule, not only the list, goes into the phase so a later fixture is classified the same way.

question: How do the PRD v2 Success tests run: 20 simultaneous attempts give one booking, and a restart keeps every booking?

options.label: API tests at the service's address, five rounds
options.consequence: Node's fetch sends 20 requests at once to http://127.0.0.1:3000 (10 with ayu's token, 10 with budi's), five rounds, the fifth with 20 different ranges that all share one quarter hour; each round gives one 201 and nineteen 409 BOOKING_CONFLICT whose conflict is the winner, and GET /api/rooms then lists one booking. The restart test books for both accounts, restarts the service, sees the old tokens answer 401, signs in again and finds every booking with its id.

options.label: one round through the dev proxy
options.consequence: Matches the PRD's wording literally, but the Vite proxy's connection handling sits between the attempts and the service, and one round proves less about a race than five.

chosen: API tests at the service's address, five rounds
why: The Success criterion is about the service and its database (booking-api@v1 G5, G6, G17); the dev proxy adds nothing to it, and the browser's view of AC-5.4 gets its own two-browser test in .5. The backend's experiment settled 20 attempts in under 100 ms, so five rounds cost under a second. A sign that the owner wants the proxy path under load would have moved the attempts behind it.

question: Which scripted test covers the criteria that turn on the backend's clock (PRD v2 AC-5.5, AC-6.2's started case, AC-6.1's booking in progress) and the one no screen reaches (AC-6.3), when the service runs on the real clock?

options.label: service tests now, the backend's replay for a started booking
options.consequence: AC-5.5: an API test books the current quarter hour (422 BOOKING_STARTED), and a browser test holds only the browser's clock five minutes before that quarter hour so the form offers it. AC-6.2's started case and AC-6.1's in-progress booking: the backend's replay of cancel-started and my-bookings-budi under its injected clock, on its real PostgreSQL, which the root `npm test` runs. AC-6.3: an API test (403 BOOKING_NOT_YOURS). No test waits for a start.

options.label: a test that waits for a booking to start
options.consequence: Proves AC-6.2's started case end to end, at up to 15 minutes of waiting on every run.

options.label: an opt-in slow script for the waiting test
options.consequence: End to end on demand, but a criterion outside `npm test` is easy to stop running.

chosen: service tests now, the backend's replay for a started booking
why: ADR-002 Decision 5 makes the backend's injected clock decide, and booking-api@v1 Validation leaves the clock-bound fixtures to the producer's replay; that replay is a scripted test against the real routes and a real PostgreSQL, run by the root `npm test`, so PRD v2 Success's 'every acceptance criterion passes in a scripted test' holds. Booking a time that has started needs no waiting at all, so AC-5.5 is end to end. The browser-clock technique was checked in the installed Chrome. Home never lists another user's booking, so AC-6.3 is reachable only through the API. An owner who reads Success as 'end to end in the browser' would want the opt-in waiting script.

question: PRD 1's 'Home within 3 seconds of Sign in' is gone from PRD v2 Success, but the shipped e2e/login.spec.ts still asserts it as AC-1.1 (Q-072): keep the assertion as a regression check, or drop it?

options.label: drop the timing assertion
options.consequence: The AC-1.1 test asserts AC-1.1 only (the right password reaches Home); the suite holds no assertion PRD v2 does not ask for, and a wall-clock limit leaves a browser suite that now also starts PostgreSQL.

options.label: keep it, renamed as a regression check
options.consequence: Catches a pathological slow-down of sign-in at no cost today, but keeps a timing assertion no requirement backs, and its failures would be read as a PRD failure.

why: PRD v2 Success names three criteria and none is a time to Home; its Goal's 'under a minute' is a person's time to find and book a room, which no script measures. The test name claims the 3 seconds is part of AC-1.1, which it never was. A PRD v2 performance target, or a history of this check catching a regression, would have kept it.

question: Which London clock-change days do the AC-4.4 browser tests use, and what do they book on them, when the service runs on the real clock and booking-api@v1 accepts starts at most 365 days ahead?

options.label: both next days, booked when within 365 days
options.consequence: The tests take the next last Sunday of March and of October strictly after today's date in London; on each they check the form and book Thames (00:30 to 02:30 on the March day, 01:30 BST to 01:30 GMT on the October day) when that start is within 365 days of the real clock. The nearer day always is (at most 217.02 days); the farther one is not for about six days in some years, and then the test checks that day's form and Rooms lines only and records an annotation.

options.label: only the next change day
options.consequence: Always bookable, but one run proves either the 23-hour or the 25-hour day, never both, for half a year at a time.

options.label: fixed dates
options.consequence: Pass, and then cannot be booked: 2026-10-25 has already gone (ADR-002 Consequences).

chosen: both next days, booked when within 365 days
why: AC-4.4 names both change days, and they fail differently (a skipped hour, a repeated hour). Scanning every hour from 2026-11-01 to 2032 found the nearer day's booking at most 217.02 days ahead, and the farther one beyond 365 days only in two spans of about six days (March 2029, October 2031); from 2026-11-01 both are bookable (147 and 364 days). Viewing a date needs no limit, since GET /api/rooms caps no range.

question: How do the browser tests know the exact strings to expect, when their dates follow the real clock?

options.label: a helper of the suite's own, Intl with an explicit zone
options.consequence: e2e/time.ts computes day ranges, quarter hours, the next change days and ADR-002 Decision 7's strings from Intl with the zone as an argument; its own tests pin ADR-002's examples and the 2027 change days. Two independent readings of ADR-002 must agree.

options.label: import the web app's time functions
options.consequence: No second implementation, but the suite then tests web/src against itself and couples to code this node does not own.

options.label: literal strings only
options.consequence: Impossible for dates that move with the clock, and wrong across London's offset change during the year.

chosen: a helper of the suite's own, Intl with an explicit zone
why: The node does not own code under web/, and a test that imports the formatter it checks proves nothing about it. web-time-display showed Intl alone reproduces every rule and PRD v2's example strings; the helper's tests pin the same strings. Where the web's mechanism is its own choice (whether Book is disabled for an empty title, say), the tests assert the PRD outcome through booking-api@v1 (no booking made) rather than the mechanism.

question: In which time zone do the browser, the test runner and the service they start run, and how is it set?

options.label: Asia/Kolkata, set in playwright.config.ts
options.consequence: The config sets `process.env.TZ = "Asia/Kolkata"` before anything reads the clock, so the runner, its workers and the service they start inherit it whichever way Playwright is started, and `use.timezoneId: "Asia/Kolkata"` sets the browser's. A time computed in the ambient zone is off by 1:30 or 5:30 from both accounts' and fails.

options.label: Asia/Kolkata, set in the npm script
options.consequence: `TZ=Asia/Kolkata playwright test` covers `npm run e2e` only; `npx playwright test` would run in the laptop's zone.

options.label: another zone
options.consequence: Any zone that is neither account's nor UTC works; a different one from the web node's tests buys nothing.

why: ADR-002 Consequences names Asia/Kolkata (+05:30) for every node's tests and the browser's zone for the browser tests; the node's Isolation strategy says the same. integration-browser-clock confirmed timezoneId gives the page Asia/Calcutta (an alias), offset -330, in the installed Chrome. The service inheriting TZ also shows it never uses its process's zone (ADR-002 Decision 3).

question: Which review tier does each appended phase take?

options.label: .3 full-review, .4 spot-check, .5 full-review
options.consequence: .3 changes the rig (database lifecycle, process groups, the time zone) and races 20 requests; .4 adds a pure helper with its own checks and Home assertions over an unchanged rig against clear contracts; .5 drives two browsers at once, holds the browser's clock and books on clock-change days.

options.label: all full-review
options.consequence: A full proposal and design for .4, whose diff is assertions and a pure helper.

why: The skill gives integrations and orchestration full-review and pure utilities spot-check; integration.2 took spot-check for assertions added over an unchanged rig, the same shape as .4. Evidence that the helper's ADR-002 reading is contested would have made .4 full-review.

question: Which cross-node phases does each appended phase wait on, when this planner sees the sibling nodes only through the contracts?

options.label: by contract: backend.4 and backend.7 for .3, web.9 for .4 and .5
options.consequence: .3 needs the service serving profile-api@v2's timeZone (simple-login.backend.4, in its produced_by) and booking-api@v1 on PostgreSQL (simple-login.backend.7, its producer); it needs no new web code, so it can land while the web lane is still building. .4 and .5 drive the new screens and wait for simple-login.web.9, the last web phase booking-api@v1 names among its consumers.

options.label: the root's join rule for every phase
options.consequence: Every appended phase waits for both lanes, so .3 cannot start, or catch the rig's breakage, until the web lane has finished.

chosen: by contract: backend.4 and backend.7 for .3, web.9 for .4 and .5
why: Contracts are the only inter-node knowledge (sibling isolation): the phase ids come from the front matter of profile-api@v2 (produced_by backend.3, backend.4) and booking-api@v1 (produced_by backend.7; consumers web.5, web.7, web.8, web.9), confirmed by Q-074. integration.2 already depended on single producer phases rather than whole lanes. If the web lane adds a phase after web.9 that changes Home or Rooms, .4 and .5 would wait for that one instead; the contracts name none.

question: Which PRD v2 sections join the node's Sources entry for hsdd/context/prd-simple-login.v2.md (Q-066)?

options.label: every story the suite proves, plus Rooms and Screens
options.consequence: The entry keeps its six sections and gains US-1, AC-2.2, AC-2.3, AC-2.5, US-3, US-4, US-5, US-6, Rooms and Screens: PRD v2 Success asks that every criterion passes in a scripted test, the tests book the four rooms and select by the Screens' words.

options.label: only the sections the new phases cite
options.consequence: AC-2.3, AC-2.5, AC-4.4, AC-5.5, AC-6.2, Rooms; US-1 and US-3, which the shipped tests prove and Success still covers, stay unlisted.

chosen: every story the suite proves, plus Rooms and Screens
why: The change-request rule appends the sections that govern the node, never replacing an entry. PRD v2 Success makes every acceptance criterion this node's to prove, so all six stories govern it; AC-2.1 and AC-2.4 are already listed, so US-2 is completed by its other three criteria rather than named twice. Goal and Left to engineering are left out: the plan tests no time to book, and the restart semantics reach the node through ADR-001 and auth-api@v1 G3.

question: simple-login.integration.4 removes the shipped 3-second check from the AC-1.1 browser test, because PRD v2 Success no longer lists 'Home within 3 seconds'. Keep that, or keep the check as a regression test?

options.label: Keep the plan; flag the omission for the owner
options.consequence: The tests follow the normative source; if product meant to keep the target, restoring it is one assertion and a PRD v2 correction.

options.label: Rework to keep the check
options.consequence: The integration node would assert a criterion no normative source states, which hsdd-phase-plan's sources rule does not support.

chosen: Keep the plan; flag the omission for the owner
why: PRD v2 is the normative source and its Success section has no time target; S08 already flagged the omission (DEC-073), and the PRD's author, writing as product for this tutorial, did not intend to drop it. That intent is not in any source the run may read, so the plan is right by its sources and the owner decides. A PRD v2 line keeping the target would have changed this.

question: S20's report lists reads outside its inputs (the shipped e2e rig and configs, the backend's package scripts, the run's records) and ran three experiments, one in the installed Chrome. Keep the output or rework?

options.label: Keep the output
options.consequence: The three integration phases stand, planned against the shipped rig they extend.

options.label: Rework without those reads
options.consequence: The phases would be planned blind to the rig and scripts they change.

why: Append mode plans against shipped code; all reads are inside the repository and none is out of bounds; the browser experiment ran the project's own Playwright. A read outside the repository would have changed this.
